There isn't one best combo. It depends on your RV's size and how you camp. The guides I read mostly compared power stations and said little about specific panels, so I've given panel sizing advice but no panel model.

**My picks by use case**

| RV use | Power station | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Weekends, small trailer or camper van | [EcoFlow Delta 3](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0DCBYMC9D/?tag=getwattlogic-20) (1,024Wh, 1,800W) | It recharges fastest in its class and can add extra batteries later. |
| Longer trips or part-time living | [Jackery Explorer 2000 v2](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0DFG2WDQH/?tag=getwattlogic-20) (2,042Wh, 2,200W, LiFePO4) | It's polished and easy to use. The guides also rated Jackery's support highest. |
| Same class, more expandable | [Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Anker%20SOLIX%20C2000%20Gen%202%202048Wh%20power%20station&tag=getwattlogic-20) (2,048Wh, 2,400W) | It expands to 4kWh and charges quickly from AC and solar. |
| Full-time, or running an AC or other heavy loads | [ALLPOWERS R4000](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh) (3,456Wh, 3,600W) | It has an RV outlet and accepts up to 2,000W of solar. Its warranty is 5 years. |

**ALLPOWERS R4000 details**
- It costs $1,319.12 with code EXTRA12, down from $1,499. The code works on orders over $1,200 and expires 11/15/2026. Dealectric tested it in the store's cart on 10/23.
- It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it's a fixture in the RV, not something you carry.
- Reaching 2,000W of solar takes panels on all three solar inputs. Each input tops out at 650W.
- The Dealectric page is an affiliate link. I haven't seen independent reviews of this unit.

**Pairing it with solar panels**
- **Check the station's solar input limit first.** Panels beyond that limit are wasted. One guide cites about 1,400W for the Jackery 2000 Plus and 1,600W for the EcoFlow Delta Pro. It lists the Bluetti AC200P at only 700W.
- **Size the battery from your loads.** One guide's example is a 150W fridge running 10 hours, which needs about 1,500Wh. A 2kWh unit gives comfortable headroom.
- **Roof or folding panels.** I'd go with roof-mounted panels if you're parked a lot. Folding panels fit short trips better. Buy panels sold for your chosen brand to avoid connector problems.

**Caveats**
- Most of these guides carry affiliate links. Their prices and specs conflict in places, and some are dated, like the AC200P. Confirm current specs and prices on the retailer's page before you buy.
- For a 30A RV hookup, check that the model has a 30A outlet. The EcoFlow Delta Pro and ALLPOWERS R4000 are listed with one. Most smaller units don't have one.

If you tell me your RV type, what you want to run (fridge, AC, CPAP) and your budget, I can narrow this to one station and a specific panel setup.

 Bluetti vs Jackery vs EcoFlow for Van Life (2026)
 If you're shopping for a portable power station for a van, RV, or off-grid rig, you've almost certainly landed on these three names. All three now build their main lineups around LiFePO4 (LFP) battery chemistry — the same durable, thermally stable chemistry recommended throughout this site — so the decision usually comes down to how each brand is positioned rather than a clear "better" or "worse" pick.
 Here's how they generally differ, and which one fits which kind of build.
 The short version
 Bluetti — best for expandability and solar input. If you're planning to grow your system over time or want to pair with a large panel array, Bluetti's higher solar input ceilings and modular accessory ecosystem make it the easiest to build around long-term.
 Jackery — best for straightforward portability and ecosystem polish. If you want something that works well out of the box with minimal setup and solid outdoor-oriented accessories, Jackery leans hardest into that use case.
 EcoFlow — best for charging speed and raw output. If fast recharge (wall or generator) matters to your routine — say, you're moving between camp spots often and want a quick top-up — EcoFlow's charging speed is its standout feature across most of its lineup.
 What actually matters for van life specifically
 Solar input ceiling. Not every power station accepts the same maximum solar wattage. If you're running a rooftop array on a van or RV — rather than a small folding panel — check the unit's rated solar input before assuming your panels will actually deliver their full output. This is one of the more common mismatch points in van builds: a well-sized panel array bottlenecked by a power station's lower solar input ceiling.
 Weight and footprint. Vans and RVs have hard limits on payload and storage space in a way that cabins and homes don't. Portability-focused designs generally trade some capacity-per-dollar for a lighter, more compact form factor — worth weighing directly against your specific rig's available space.
 Expandability. Some models in each brand's lineup support add-on battery modules to grow capacity after your initial purchase, rather than requiring a full unit swap. If you expect your power needs to grow — adding a fridge, later going full-time — this is worth checking before you commit to a fixed-capacity unit.
 Charging speed. How you actually recharge matters more than the spec sheet suggests. If you're relying primarily on solar, recharge speed from a wall outlet or generator matters less. If you're moving frequently and topping up from campground power or a generator between stops, faster recharge times translate directly into less downtime.
 Chemistry: why LiFePO4 matters
 Across all three brands, the main current-generation lineups have shifted to LiFePO4 chemistry, which offers a meaningfully longer cycle life (commonly rated in the thousands of charge cycles to 80% capacity) than older lithium-ion designs, along with better thermal stability. Some older or lower-tier models — across any of these brands — may still use older chemistry, so it's worth confirming the battery chemistry of the specific model you're considering rather than assuming based on brand alone.
 How to actually decide
 The honest answer is that all three brands are credible, and the "best" one depends on your specific loadout and habits more than brand loyalty. That's exactly what the calculator on this site solves — instead of matching your build to a brand's marketing positioning, it sizes your battery capacity from your actual devices and usage, so you know what capacity, solar input, and inverter rating you actually need before you start comparing specific models.

 Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Bluetti: Ultimate Brand Comparison 2026
 Updated: August 2026 • 10 min read
 If you're shopping for a portable power station in 2026, three names keep coming up: Jackery, EcoFlow, and Bluetti. They're the big three — together they control roughly 70% of the portable power station market. But they take very different approaches to design, pricing, and features. This is the comparison I wish I'd read before buying my first power station. Let's break it down.
 📊 June 2026 Market Update: Prices have stabilized after supply chain improvements. Jackery holds steady at $1,899 for the 2000 Plus. EcoFlow launched the Delta 3 series in Q1 2026 but the Delta Pro remains better value for home backup. Bluetti's AC200P at $1,299 is the most affordable 2,000Wh station from a major brand — though the 700W solar input limit hasn't improved. Anker (not in this three-way comparison but worth watching) now competes aggressively at the $1,599 price point with the SOLIX F2000.
[Check current prices on Amazon →](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=08191509-20)
 Brand Overviews
 Jackery — The Pioneer
 Founded in 2012 in California, Jackery basically created the portable power station category as we know it. They're the most recognized brand and the one your neighbor has probably heard of. Their design philosophy is Apple-like: polished, user-friendly, and premium-priced. Jackery stations rarely have the best specs on paper, but they consistently deliver the smoothest out-of-box experience. Their Explorer series is iconic and their expansion system is the most elegant on the market.
 EcoFlow — The Innovator
 Founded in 2017 by former DJI engineers, EcoFlow came in hot with the Delta series and its game-changing X-Boost and multi-charge technology. They aim for the highest specs: fastest charging, highest output, most features. EcoFlow's ecosystem extends beyond power stations into smart home panels, portable air conditioners (the Wave 2), and even a battery-powered fridge. If you want cutting-edge tech and maximum expandability, EcoFlow is the brand.
 Bluetti — The Value King
 Bluetti (formerly MaxOak) launched the AC200 in 2020 and disrupted the market with aggressive pricing. Their philosophy is simple: give you the most watt-hours and the most outlets for the least money. Bluetti stations sometimes lag on software polish, solar input speed, and app features — but they're almost always the best deal in terms of raw capacity per dollar.

 Build Quality and Design
 Jackery wins on fit and finish. The Explorer 2000 Plus feels like a premium consumer electronics product — smooth edges, tight seams, satisfying button clicks. The orange-accented design is instantly recognizable. Everything about the physical experience feels intentional.
 EcoFlow goes for rugged utility. The Delta Pro is built like a tank — thick plastic, reinforced corners, heavy-duty wheels. It's designed to be moved in and out of job sites, RVs, and garages. It's not pretty, but it's durable.
 Bluetti is utilitarian. The AC200P has a boxy, functional design with slightly cheaper-feeling plastics. The handle is basic. But nothing feels fragile or poorly assembled — it's just not as polished as the other two.
 Winner: Jackery for looks, EcoFlow for durability.
 App and Software Experience
 EcoFlow has the best app by a wide margin. Real-time energy monitoring, customizable charge/discharge schedules, X-Boost toggling, firmware OTA updates, and Alexa/Google Home integration. You can see per-port power draw and set battery reserve levels for outages. It's genuinely useful.
 Jackery comes second with a clean, reliable app. WiFi + Bluetooth, remote monitoring, port toggling, and firmware updates. It's simpler than EcoFlow's but more reliable — I've never had a connection drop with the Jackery app.
 Bluetti is a distant third. Bluetooth only, no WiFi, no remote monitoring, no scheduling, no OTA firmware updates. You have to load firmware via SD card. The app shows basic info (battery %, input/output watts) but that's about it.
 Winner: EcoFlow (by a mile).
 Charging Speed
 EcoFlow is the undisputed champion here. The Delta Pro charges at up to 3,000W via 240V AC (0-100% in 1.8 hours), takes up to 1,600W solar, and can combine AC + solar for up to 6,500W total input. That's a full charge in about 35 minutes if you max everything out.
 Jackery is solid: 1,800W AC charging (2 hours to full) and 1,400W solar input. Not the fastest, but more than adequate.
 Bluetti is slow: 400W AC charging stock (5-6 hours), or 800W with a second charger. Solar input is capped at 700W. If you camp in cloudy conditions or need quick turnaround between uses, this is a real limitation.
 Winner: EcoFlow.
